Transport Angels

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
(Open on a vast, star-filled night sky, then pan down to the dimly lit, labyrinthine streets of a Cape Town township. The air is cold, the shadows deep.)
The Call in the Dark
The official vehicles won't go here. The police and ambulance services draw a line on the map, a boundary dictated by fear and danger. But beyond that line, in the deepest, most underserved corners of the Western Cape, are children fighting battles no child should face—battling life-limiting illnesses.
Every morning, before the city truly wakes, two men receive their dispatch. They are Sonwabo and Humbert, and they are the drivers of a different kind of train: the Super Sam Hero Transport.
This is not just a drive; it's a commitment to the impossible. For over 382,510 km, they have taken on the mantle of essential lifelines, safely moving 13,491 young patients to the care they desperately need.
(Cut to a shot of a clean, vehicle navigating a deeply potholed, dark road. The contrast is stark.)

The Super Sam Express
Inspired by the sheer, unwavering hope of the "Polar Express," our story begins and ends with the journey.
Imagine the quiet ritual: Sonwabo or Humbert, a beacon in the pre-dawn dark, carefully pulling up to a shack or a small, isolated house. The streets are menacing; the threat of crime is constant. Yet, they step out, calm and utterly focused. They don't just open a door; they usher a child into a sanctuary.
In the back of the Paedspal vehicle the world of illness and danger momentarily fades. For these young VIPs, this vehicle is a bubble of warmth, dignity, and unwavering safety. The drivers' warm smiles and gentle hands lift children in wheelchairs, secure prams, and transform a terrifying necessity into a journey of respect.
(Cut to a close-up of a driver's hand on a child's shoulder, offering a word of encouragement. The child looks fragile but offers a small smile.)
The Unseen Route
We need a ride-along not just to document the logistics, but to witness the courage. This is the heart of the "Carte Blanche" treatment: putting the viewer in the passenger seat as Sonwabo or Humbert deliberately cross the lines others won't.
The Danger: We will visually contrast the polished hospitals of Cape Town with the brutal reality of the routes—the tension in the air, the need for hyper-vigilance.
The Mission: Every trip is an act of resistance against despair. More than a driver, they are a counsellor, a friend, a steady anchor for overwhelmed parents and frightened children seeking vital medical appointments, therapy sessions, and psychosocial support.
The Resilience: Through candid interviews in the quiet moments between pickups, we’ll uncover the deeply human side of these drivers. What compels them to face down the danger, day after day? The answer lies in the hope they deliver.
Where it all started : We speak to the founder Melissa- This is an important interview for context and to highlight the wonderful work done.
(Close with a shot of the sun rising over shacks . The Super Sam Hero Transport is seen driving toward the light, carrying its precious cargo.)
This is not a story about statistics; it is a profound testament to what is possible when pure, courageous empathy refuses to acknowledge boundaries—a journey of dignity forged on the most dangerous roads.

Script:


(Govan) Early in the morning, while Cape Town still sleeps, two drivers are already on the road. For them, each day is more than just another drive – it’s a risk.



(Humbert Kordom) This is not a job for me. This is my calling. The kids, when I pass the schools, they’re screaming, “Hi Sam! Hi Superhero! Hi!”



(Govan) They’re not policemen or paramedics. Yet for many families, they are the difference between uncertainty and hope – getting sick children safely to hospital.



(Sonwabo Mandindi) I know that I have a purpose. And me doing this, I'm touching so many lives.



(News Bulletin 1) Two people were shot dead, and three others were injured in a mass shooting incident in Gugulethu.



(News Bulletin 2) Ramping gang violence is affecting the daily lives of residents.



(News Bulleting 3) Western Cape police have identified four of five bodies discovered in Khayelitsha.



(Govan) In this city, fear draws invisible borders.



(Govan) Streets so dangerous even emergency services won’t go there… Beyond these lines, families struggle to reach life-saving medical care.



(Govan) For children living with a serious illness, one missed appointment can mean losing out on vital treatment. In the townships of the Western Cape, the struggle isn’t getting access to care – it’s the cost of getting there.



(Govan) Poverty, violence, and high unemployment mean many families can’t afford the trip to hospital.



(Govan) But one initiative is changing that. Across townships in Cape Town, their bright minibuses have become a familiar sight. Super Sam Hero Transport has given sick children and their caregivers free rides to life-saving appointments at state hospitals.



(Melissa Williams-Platt) Children weren't coming to the clinic. They didn't have money for transport, you know. The three taxis, the three busses… It's just too much for the mums who often had a child in a wheelchair.



(Govan) Run by NGO Footprints for Sam, co-founder Melissa Williams-Platt started Super Sam Hero Transport after seeing children miss critical appointments while her son, Sam, was at the Red Cross Children’s Hospital. After he died, she turned grief into action.



(Govan) Tell me: why did you decide to invest in transport?



(Melissa Williams-Platt) As I started speaking to moms, if a child has a chronic condition, they have to go regularly – whether it may be back to hospital or to clinics. And often it's a choice: do I put food on the table, or do I go into hospital?



(Govan) With just two minibuses and a pair of brave drivers, over 8 000 children and their families no longer have to make that choice.



(Humbert Kordom) Good morning! Morning, morning!



(Govan) How are you doing?



(Humbert Kordom) Good, good.



(Govan) My name is Govan.



(Humbert) Humbert.



(Govan Subtitles) So, you’re the guys who take the children to the hospital?



(Humbert Kordom) Subtitles) That’s right.



(Govan) I’ll be spending the next few days with two of their drivers.



(Govan) Let’s get in before the traffic gets too bad.



(Govan) Humbert Kordom – known as Humbie – has been behind the wheel for over eight years. Today, he’ll be taking two young patients to Red Cross Children’s Hospital.



(Govan) So, where are we going first, Mr Humbie?



(Humbert Kordom) We're going to Khayelitsha first. And then, after that, Gugulethu.



(Govan) Humbert is on edge. Khayelitsha and Gugulethu are hijacking hotspots… And he’s faced his share of close calls.



(Humbert Kordom) The guy was standing in front of me with a gun and shouted at me, “Get out! Get out!”



(Govan) And you had kids in the bus?



(Humbert Kordom) Kids in the bus! And I just bent and drive, and he jumped out of the way. The kids were crying. They were crying in the van. I'm still seeing a psychologist about this hijacking.



(Govan) Despite the risks, Humbert remains determined to make every pickup.



(Govan) We finally arrive… Humbert guides me through narrow, often dangerous alleyways to reach the family.



(Humbert Kordom) This is the house.



(Govan Subtitles) Hello. How are you?



(Govan) Endinakho has a chronic lung condition and partial blindness. She and her grandmother, Fundiswa Makeleni, depend on Humbert for every hospital trip.



(Govan) How has that journey been?



(Fundiswa Makeleni Subtitles) Khayelitsha is very dangerous, but Sam’s minibuses… They take initiative and come to pick me up and also drop me off, knowing very well how dangerous it is in Khayelitsha. All they care about is Endinako’s life.



(Govan) Just 15 minutes from Khayelitsha, the need is just as urgent.



(Govan) Alright, sir. Where are we heading now?



(Humbert Kordom) We’re heading to Gugulethu, the Pietersen family. Jayden Pietersen.



(Humbert Kordom) He got a lot of severe illnesses. He’s in a wheelchair. So, the mom was also struggling with transport for them, to get them to the hospital and from the hospital.



(Govan) Jayden has cerebral palsy – his mother, Nicole Pietersen, cares for him full-time. Without reliable transport, he often missed vital hospital appointments.



(Govan) When you used to take Jayden to the hospital with the public transport, did you leave the wheelchair at home?



(Nicole Pietersen) Yes. Yes. I left the wheelchair at home. And then I would carry him all the way.



(Govan) And, I mean, that's not ideal. But it's also not comfortable for him.



(Govan) The bonds these drivers form with the children run deep. Sonwabo Mandindi, another driver, builds lasting connections even through the heartbreak of the job.



(Govan) Is it hard working with the children who have different diseases?



(Sonwabo Mandindi) You know, we create a bond. Sometimes the kids are born within a month – they realise the child has a condition. Then from then, after a month, then you start seeing the child almost every second week.



(Govan) Yeah, which you get pretty close.



(Sonwabo Mandindi) Some of them are even five years now.



(Govan) Have you lost any of the patients that you transport?



(Sonwabo Mandindi) Yho, a lot of children have lost their lives. When the day comes, it's emotional. And the way it's so emotional – sometimes you feel like you don't want to continue doing this work. You don't want to continue, but you know you need to be there for others who are still fighting.



(Govan) Arriving at the hospital can be stressful and filled with anxiety. But Humbert and Sonwabo are always just a call or text away.



(Govan) Super Sam Hero Transport partners with Red Cross Children’s Hospital. Professor Mignon McCulloch has seen the difference.



(Govan) How often do kids miss appointments?



(Professor Mignon McCulloch) We make plans on the management and decide whether we need to do any surgery on them or add any new medication or remove any medication. And so, if kids actually miss their appointment, it has a major impact on the quality of their health care. Having a taxi service that's quite expensive, is very overcrowded… If a child's on drugs that suppress the immune system…



(Govan) So, it's also a health risk to take public transport back if you've had like…



(Professor Mignon McCulloch) It can be if you've been on medication that suppress your immune system. And Sam’s van offers us many services; safe, reliable transport, also a safe environment for them to be in.



(Govan) It's midday and Humbert’s day is coming to an end. As he completes his final drop-offs, one quiet truth remains – even a driver can change a life, one trip at a time.



(Humbert Kordom) It’s so unbelievable to see what Sam’s buses can do, what me as a driver can do. The impact into others’ lives by making a big difference. I am proud of that.



(Govan) No. You should be proud!



(Sonwabo Mandindi) Me doing this, I know for a fact, even if I’m broken inside… But if I see another child who’s fighting, it gives me hope that at least I’m giving life to another person.

The Danger: We will visually contrast the polished hospitals of Cape Town with the brutal reality of the routes—the tension in the air, the need for hyper-vigilance. The Mission: Every trip is an act of resistance against despair. More than a driver, they are a counsellor, a friend, a steady anchor for overwhelmed parents and frightened children seeking vital medical appointments, therapy sessions, and psychosocial support. The Resilience: Through candid interviews in the quiet moments between pickups, we’ll uncover the deeply human side of these drivers. What compels them to face down the danger, day after day? The answer lies in the hope they deliver. Where it all started : We speak to the founder Melissa- This is an important interview for context and to highlight the wonderful work done. (Close with a shot of the sun rising over shacks . The Super Sam Hero Transport is seen driving toward the light, carrying its precious cargo.) This is not a story about statistics; it is a profound testament to what is possible when pure, courageous empathy refuses to acknowledge boundaries—a journey of dignity forged on the most dangerous roads.
